assessments.reasoning: Authenticity. The archival scan visually identifies Clocksin, the ZIP title and January 1983 with subsequent revisions. The archive’s Prolog-X documents section directly links the exact file. Integrity. The independently retrieved public file matched the frozen SHA-256 e39c1b29d389a0ae9b43301054470c807406c7ff63a6071e953ad38b0d04c192. Relevance and interpretation at Physical PDF page 1, Opening paragraph after the title and author. The opening paragraph identifies Prolog-X as implementing Prolog and using a separately named abstract ZIP machine. The following Pointers discussion refers to Prolog-X as the present simulator. Applicability. The cited author or publisher describes the same frozen historical or documented scope. Contradiction check. The scan identifies an implementation and the virtual machine it uses. The archive's NIP account suggests a version lineage and leaves product boundaries open.

challenge.method: Compare the scanned opening and software-simulator paragraph with the archive's Prolog-X and NIP sections. Test equal identity between ZIP and Prolog-X, and whether the contemporary NIP branch invalidates the narrower identification.
challenge.results: The scan identifies an implementation and the virtual machine it uses. The archive's NIP account suggests a version lineage and leaves product boundaries open.

limitations: The artifact is the January 1983 ZIP design with subsequent revisions. Registry state concerns the reference identity, without asserting current maintenance.
The artifact establishes the January 1983 design as subsequently revised. It does not establish current maintenance, NIP equivalence or general compatibility.
